power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Diet can impact on physical and mental health, but to what extent do people believe this?
Health psychology theory proposes that beliefs about the impact diet has on health likely shape behaviour.
Yet, diet-health beliefs have not been systematically studied and methodology used in existing research is limited.

This two-part study aimed to explore UK adults' beliefs about the impact diet has on short-term and long-term physical and mental health conditions, and to conduct initial development and validation of a scale to measure diet-health beliefs.
An initial 20-item scale was completed by a general population sample of 399 UK adults online.
Results show that participants had inconsistent beliefs about the impact diet has on long-term and short-term physical health outcomes.
Participants tended not to believe that diet impacts mental health.

Next, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis of survey responses indicated a 15-item two-factor (physical health, mental health) scale provided the most statistically appropriate measure of diet-health beliefs.
The scale was found to be reliable at both full (ω = ₜ 0.93) and subscale level (factor 1: physical health, ωₜ = 0.90, factor 2: mental health, ωₜ = 0.93).
Convergent, divergent and test-retest validity assessments confirmed the scale had acceptable validity.

The scale could be used to investigate whether beliefs about the impact of diet on health shape dietary behaviour and investigate the effectiveness of interventions designed to change diet-health beliefs.
A strong body of evidence has long supported the fundamental role that diet plays in maintaining and promoting physical health.
Eating a healthy diet can help prevent future health problems (Cena & Calder, 2020).

Methods

text.text: Potential survey items were collated from existing measures assessing dietdisease knowledge (Glick et al., 2024; Guan & Chen, 2024; Sapp & Jensen, 1997; Sapp & Weng, 2007; Smith et al., 2000).

text.text: Collated items were assessed for relevance to short-term and long-term diet-related health conditions by three researchers at the University of Liverpool.

Twenty items were included in the initial survey (see online supplementary materials, Table 1), assessing beliefs about long-term health impacts of diet (on physical health n=8, e.g. heart disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer, dementia, and on mental health n=3, e.g. anxiety, depression) and short-term health impacts of diet (on physical health n=5, e.g. cholesterol, blood pressure, digestive health and on mental health n=4, e.g. mood, stress, self-esteem).

text.text: Participants were asked to rate their level of agreement with each of the items (e.g.
'The food a person eats influences their likelihood of developing heart disease in the long-term') using a seven-point Likert scale.

text.text: Participants tended to believe that diet impacted items relating to longer-term physical health conditions (see Table 2).

text.text: For example, there was a high degree of certainty in belief (scores of 6 or 7) that heart disease (76% with high degree of certainty), type 2 diabetes (81%), obesity (89%) and general physical health (83%) were affected by diet.

Beliefs in other long-term physical health outcomes were more variable; 38% of participants believed with a high degree of certainty that diet affects the likelihood of developing cancer and 45% believed with a high degree of certainty that diet affects how long a person lives.
Participants tended to believe diet affects short-term physical health: cholesterol (72% with high degree of certainty), blood sugar (87%), and digestive health (83%).

Few participants tended to believe with a high degree of certainty that studied physical health outcomes were not affected by diet, although 5% of participants believed this to be the case for cancer.

Beliefs about diet influencing long-term mental health conditions were more mixed. 26% of participants believed with a high degree of certainty that diet influences mental health, and fewer people believed with a high degree of certainty that anxiety and depression were affected by diet (12% and 17%, respectively).

Beliefs about the influence of diet on short-term mental health conditions were more moderate, with 35% believing with a high degree of certainty that diet impacts wellbeing, mood (45%) and self-esteem (30%).

Of all mental health items, levels of belief certainty for items not being impacted by diet were highest for anxiety (24% believed with certainty that this was not impacted by diet), depression (16%), stress (11%) and mental health in general (10%).

For relevance, validators were asked to score each item on a five-point scale, with the options 'not relevant', 'somewhat relevant', 'quite relevant', 'relevant' and 'highly relevant'.

Diet-health belief scale scores were compared with health fatalism scores.

Factor 1 (physical health) demonstrated a small but significant negative correlation, r(395) = -0.11, p = 0.04, (95% CI = -0.20 to -0.01), indicating that stronger diet-health beliefs about impacts on physical health are modestly associated with lower fatalistic attitudes.

text.text: In the first part of the present research, we created and administered a 20item scale to examine beliefs about the impact of diet on multiple aspects of short-term and longer-term physical and mental health in a sample of UK adults.
Participants tended to believe with a high degree of certainty that diet affects some longer-term physical health conditions such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.
Beliefs about diet's influence on day-to-day physical health (e.g. cholesterol, blood sugar, digestive health) were similarly strong.

In contrast, beliefs about the impact of diet on short-term and longer-term mental health outcomes were far more variable and a large proportion of participants did not believe with any certainty that diet affects long-term mental health, particularly anxiety and depression.
Although participants tended to believe with certainty that diet affects physical health outcomes, there was significant variability across different outcomes.
For example, fewer than 1 in 2 surveyed UK adults believed with a high degree of certainty that diet affects the likelihood of developing cancer.
Similarly, most participants did not believe with certainty that diet affects life expectancy.
This potentially highlights a lack of understanding of how diet can impact cancer risk and lead to early mortality (Key et al., 2020; Steck & Murphy, 2020).
text.formatted: This potentially highlights a lack of understanding of how diet can impact cancer risk and lead to early mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Key et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Steck & Murphy, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Further, the lack of certainty regarding the impact of diet on longevity is an interesting contradiction to the certainty in beliefs about the impact of diet on multiple life-limiting physical health conditions such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

This could be partly explained by the human tendency to be present-biased (Liu et al., 2014), faith in medical treatment, or a disconnect in knowledge that long-term physical health conditions lead to early mortality.
text.formatted: This could be partly explained by the human tendency to be present-biased <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Liu et al., 2014)</ref>, faith in medical treatment, or a disconnect in knowledge that long-term physical health conditions lead to early mortality.

text.text: Participant beliefs about the impact of diet on mental health outcomes were less certain than those about physical health.

For example, just over 1 in 4 adults believed with certainty that diet impacts longer-term mental health, with even fewer believing with certainty that diet impacts anxiety (12%), depression (17%) and stress (23%).

Conversely, recent systematic reviews show associations between poor diet and mental health conditions (Chen et al., 2021; Firth et al., 2019) and mental health guidance provided to the general public highlights the importance of diet (Mental Health Foundation, 2026; NHS Professionals, 2026).

text.text: Belief about the impact of diet on dementia were very mixed, with most participants (35%) unsure whether diet impacts the likelihood of developing dementia, and the number of people believing with certainty that diet impacts dementia risk almost exactly matching those disbelieving diet affects dementia risk (15% and 16% respectively).

These findings highlight a lack of understanding of the likely role that diet plays in dementia risk (Arora et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2020), and are similar to findings of an Alzheimer's Research UK survey showing only 25% of adults listed diet as a risk factor for developing dementia (Alzheimer's Research UK, 2026).

text.text: These findings may also reflect the differentiation in beliefs that participants have about diet's impact on physical vs. mental health.

Whilst dementia was categorised as a long-term physical health impact during scale creation, factor analysis using participant survey responses showed that dementia clearly loaded onto the subscale relating to mental health.
Therefore, participants may less strongly believe diet affects dementia because it is not typically thought of as a physical health condition.
Participants also completed a task in which they ranked diet alongside other influences on health.
Although participants ranked diet quite highly (54% ranked it in the top five factors), they believed that smoking was a far greater influence on health (80% ranked it in the top five factors).
Comparison of responses to beliefs about the impact of smoking on physical health to a similar question about diet produced similar results.

This is a notable finding, given that recent evidence suggests that at population level, poor diet has overtaken smoking as the leading cause of preventable death, notably death attributable to cardiovascular disease (Hull et al., 2025; Norouzzadeh et al., 2024).

Nonetheless, questions previously used to assess diet-health awareness show similarly variable results to the findings presented here, although potentially highlight improvements over time.

text.text: The present research developed and validated a new 15-item scale to measure diet-health beliefs.

Factor analysis did not support our original hypothesis of a four-factor structure (i.e. physical vs. mental health, long term vs. short term health impacts) as factor loadings did not differentiate between short-term and long-term health conditions.

Exploratory factor analysis indicated that a two-factor solution (factor 1: physical health, factor 2: mental health) provided the most accurate representation of the data, with strong primary loadings and minimal cross-loading after the removal of five items.
Confirmatory factor analysis further supported this structure, demonstrating good model fit and significant standardised loadings for all retained items.

These findings suggest that diet-health beliefs are multidimensional, with individuals differentiating between physical and mental aspects of health when evaluating the impact of diet, but not necessarily shorter-vs. longer-term outcomes.
The 15-item scale demonstrated excellent internal reliability, at full scale and subscale level.

Evidence supported convergent validity; diet-health belief scores were positively associated with other ratings of how strongly diet influences health, aligning with theoretical expectations that individuals who recognise the health consequences of diet also tend to recognise other established physical health risks.

Discriminant validity was also supported, with negligible or small correlations with health fatalism and Average Variance Extracted values exceeding shared variance between factors, indicating that the two constructs are empirically distinct.
Test-retest reliability was good for the total scale, but only moderate for the individual sub-scales (ICCs = 0.56).
This was lower than anticipated and may be explained by relative strength of diet-health beliefs being prone to some fluctuations over time.
Further research examining test-retest reliability of the scale would now be informative.

These initial development and validation results indicate that the diet-health belief scale could be used in future research to examine population variability in diet-health beliefs, factors that shape diet-health beliefs, the underlying reasons why diet-health beliefs vary from person-to-person and/or testing of interventions designed to change diet-health beliefs.

Although a proportion of participants in the present study tended to agree that diet affects a range of health outcomes, there was considerable variability within and between individual health outcomes.
It is therefore feasible that a significant subset of the population does not believe that diet affects health or does not strongly believe that diet has a meaningful impact on health.
The scale could therefore also be used to examine whether individual differences in diet-health beliefs impact on behaviour and diet quality.
Importantly, diet-health beliefs did not differ significantly across gender, ethnicity, and education level.
Further research could explore whether stronger diet health-beliefs in younger age groups and higher BMI categories are replicated in larger samples.
Despite the strengths of this study, several limitations should be acknowledged.
Although the sample varied by education level, age and gender, the majority of participants identified as white.
Despite this being representative of the UK population, it limits generalisability to more ethnically diverse populations.

The sample was randomly selected from participants that had previously completed an online study examining the impact of nutrition information labels on hypothetical food selection, and thus participants may have been more interested in diet and health than the general population.
Because our focus was on scale development in the general population, we did not stratify recruitment by current physical or mental health condition.

Whilst we would anticipate prevalence of individual physical and mental health conditions would be relatively low in the sampled population, we did not measure diagnosis of physical or mental health conditions in participants.

Future work could address these limitations by purposefully sampling participants with different health conditions, in order to be able to formally compare whether beliefs about diet and health differ by health status.
Further validation of this newly developed scale outside of the general population and in samples characterised by having existing physical and/or mental health conditions would also be of value.

The cross-sectional design used in the present research limits causal inference, preventing conclusions about the potential directionality of associations between diet-health beliefs and related constructs.

text.text: It would therefore be informative to understand whether first vs. third-person anchoring affects responses for diet-health beliefs.

Based on typical first vs. third-person effects (Fontaine & Smith, 1995), we would hypothesise that participants may be even less likely to believe diet impacts on health when reporting about one's own diet and health, as opposed to others (as in the present study).

text.text: These limitations highlight directions for future research.

Given that most people in the UK do not meet national nutritional recommendations (Office for Health Improvements and Disparities, 2025) investigating how diet-health beliefs correlate with dietary choices could now be informative.

Thus, an important next step would be to examine the scale's predictive validity, particularly in relation to real-world food purchasing, habitual dietary intake, eating out-of-home and responses to interventions designed to promote healthier eating such as nutrition labelling.

As scale wording was assessed for clarity by psychology researchers, think-aloud work may also help to clarify that scale wording was understood as intended by participants, especially as terms such as 'mental wellbeing' may be open to individual interpretation (Padilla & Leighton, 2017).

text.text: Longitudinal research could explore how diet-health beliefs evolve over time and whether they shift in response to public health messaging, interventions, educational campaigns or changes in personal health status.
Given the variability in beliefs about diet and mental health, qualitative work may help clarify how individuals conceptualise the relationship between diet and psychological wellbeing.
Validation studies outside of the UK would help determine whether the two-factor structure is stable across different cultural and dietary contexts.

Conclusion This study provides evidence that the newly developed Diet-Health Belief Scale is a reliable, valid, and conceptually coherent measure of beliefs about the influence of diet on physical and mental health.

Participants tended to believe with some certainty that diet impacts multiple aspects of physical health, but did not tend to strongly believe that diet affects longevity and most mental health outcomes.
Together, these findings indicate that the scale is well suited for use in future research and may serve as a valuable tool for understanding diet-health beliefs.
